column1: 1. Bowl diameter directly affects volume and bass response. Larger bowl = louder, more bass.
2. Goatskin tension is critical — too tight = thin/bright, too loose = muddy/quiet. Let dry completely before final tuning.
3. String lengths are approximations based on a linear neck curve. Actual lengths depend on your neck curvature and bridge position.
4. %Breaking over 80% risks breakage. If any string exceeds this, increase vibrating length (lower bridge, longer neck) or use heavier gauge.
5. Wound strings (#18-21) use 2.5× nylon density factor. Adjust wound start point if %breaking is too high on plain nylon bass strings.
6. Segmented bowl: same miter sled + ring-stack method as Ashiko and Conga sheets. Stave bowl: faster but less decorative.
7. Traditional kora uses calabash gourd — segmented/stave wood bowl is Tony's CNC adaptation for consistency and durability.
8. Electric version: piezo under bridge captures all 21 strings. Position affects tone — center = balanced, offset = favors one hand.
9. Havlena build reference: smaller proportions (16" bowl, 49" neck). Full-size traditional kora is larger (20" bowl, 51" neck).
10. String 21 doubles string 20 (both F3) — traditional kora has 11 right-hand + 10 left-hand strings with the lowest note shared.

11. TODO: Revisit treble string stress — strings 1-5 and #18 exceed 80% breaking. Options: reduce B10 (treble tension), lengthen F59:F63/F76 (vibrating length), or switch to fluorocarbon (higher σ_break).

Origin: Mande peoples of West Africa (Manding empire, ~13th–14th c.). Strongest living tradition in Gambia, Senegal, Guinea, Mali, Guinea-Bissau, Burkina Faso, Côte d'Ivoire.
Etymology: 'Kora' likely from Mandinka. Played by jali/jeli/griot — hereditary musician-historians. Core families: Kouyaté, Diabaté, Kuyateh, Suso, Cissokho.
First European description: Mungo Park, 1799 (Travels in the Interior Districts of Africa). Earliest extant instruments date to early 19th c.
Tunings: Silaba (F major), Tomora (F Lydian), Sauta (F Mixolydian), Hardino (F Dorian-ish). All built around F3 fundamental, two ranks straddling the bridge.

Governing law: Mersenne–Taylor — f = (1/2L)·√(T/μ), with μ = ρ·π·(d/2)² for monofilament, μ × wound-factor (~2.5) for wound bass.
Stiffness correction (real strings, not ideal): f_n = n·f0·√(1 + B·n²),  B = π²·E·I / (T·L²),  I = π·d⁴/64. Bass strings need this — treble nylon ~negligible.
Damping: exponential decay e^(−t/τ), τ depends on bridge admittance + skin head losses. Two-mass coupled oscillator (string + bridge + membrane) captures sympathetic tones.
Bridge physics: notched bridge transfers vibration into goatskin head — head acts as a low-Q radiator. Membrane modes: J_{m,n} Bessel zeros / (π·a) × √(T_skin/σ_skin).
%Breaking (independent of d): %break = ρ·4·L²·f² / (σ_break·g) × 100. Cross-references column G in string schedule above.
Wolfram functions: NDSolve[ ] for damped wave equation on the string; PlayString[Sound[ ]] for synthesized pluck; SoundNote, AudioGenerator, Spectrogram, Periodogram.
Wolfram functions: BesselJZero[m,n] for circular membrane modes; ContourPlot3D[BesselJ[m,k r] Cos[m θ]] for mode-shape animations of the skin head.
Wolfram functions: FourierTrigSeries / Fourier / PowerSpectralDensity for harmonic content of recorded plucks; LinearSolve / Eigensystem for coupled string-bridge model.
Bowl: hemispherical-ish (segmented or stave). Parameterize as Surface of Revolution with profile r(z). Segmented version = RegionUnion of mitered prisms.
Neck: long cylindrical/octagonal stick. Bridge sits on goatskin head, tilted forward. String anchor: leather rings sliding on neck for tuning.
String geometry: each string runs from anchor → over bridge notch → to a tying point at the foot. Vibrating length = bridge-notch to anchor.
Wolfram items: ParametricPlot3D[{r[z] Cos[θ], r[z] Sin[θ], z},…] for bowl; RevolutionPlot3D; RegionPlot3D for chamber volume.

Strings — Nylon: ρ=0.04155 lb/in³, σ_break=44,600 psi. Fluorocarbon (PVDF): ρ≈0.0635, σ_break≈55,000 (higher tension capacity, brighter).
Strings — Wound bass: nylon core + nylon/silver-plated copper winding. Effective ρ ≈ 2.5× plain nylon (sheet uses this).
Bowl woods: Maple ρ=705 kg/m³ E=12.6 GPa; Walnut ρ=610 E=11.6; Cherry ρ=560 E=10.3; Mahogany ρ=590 E=10.1. Bowl mass ≠ tone driver — head + bridge dominate.
Goatskin: σ_skin (areal density) ~0.4–0.7 kg/m², T_skin tunable by lacing tension. Head mode 0,1 should sit ~30–40% above F3 fundamental (sympathetic ring without masking).
Correction factors: stiffness inharmonicity B (above); finite-bridge admittance shifts f by 1–3% depending on neck/bridge stiffness; humidity affects nylon by ±0.5% over a season.
